panels.title: Ingest rate
panels.description: Durable events per second — counted after the broker acknowledged, so this is throughput, not arrival rate.

panels.title: Rejection rate
panels.description: Events refused at ingest, per second. Any sustained value means a producer is shipping something wolfram will not take.

panels.title: Consumer lag
panels.description: Committed offset vs the log end, summed over every partition. Growing is the signal; the absolute number is not.

panels.title: Dead-letter rate
panels.description: Records routed to the DLQ, per second over 15 minutes. Any sustained non-zero value is a page (runbook 6.3).

panels.title: Partition headroom
panels.description: Months from now that already have a partition. Below 2 the fix has to happen this month; at 0 every insert is dead-lettered (runbook 6.2 step 4).

panels.title: Targets up
panels.description: Prometheus scrape targets answering. Three is the whole fleet.

panels.title: Accepted events by type
panels.description: `ingest.events.received`, split by CloudEvents `type`. Stacked because the total is the throughput number and the split is which producer moved.

panels.title: Rejections by reason
panels.description: `ingest.events.rejected`. The reason set is closed by construction: malformed, invalid-attributes, invalid-payload, unknown-type, too-large. `too-large` and the two invalid-* reasons are producer bugs; a clock skew shows up as invalid-attributes.

panels.title: Kafka produce latency
panels.description: Broker acknowledgement latency by percentile, from `kafka.produce.latency` buckets. A rising p50 is broker pressure across the board; a rising p99 over a flat p50 is one slow partition leader. Buckets run 1ms–2.5s — anything at the top of the range is failing, not slow.

panels.title: Produce outcomes
panels.description: There is no separate produce-error counter: `outcome="failure"` on the latency timer is the broker-error rate, and every one of those was a 503 to a client whose event was NOT published.

panels.title: Consumer lag by partition
panels.description: `consume.group.lag`, from an AdminClient comparing committed offsets against listOffsets(LATEST) — not the client's own records-lag-max, which reads zero during a rebalance and vanishes when the consumer is down. One partition diverging from the rest is a stuck assignment, not a throughput problem.

panels.title: Batch write latency
panels.description: `consume.batch.latency` percentiles — the batch INSERT's wall clock. Rising with batches at the cap means the write side is the bottleneck: check Postgres connections, locks, autovacuum on the hot partition and the four GIN indexes. The 5s top bucket is where a batch starts threatening `max.poll.interval.ms` and a rebalance.

panels.title: Rows persisted and de-duplicated
panels.description: Duplicates are NORMAL for an at-least-once pipeline — the write deduplicates on the CloudEvents identity — so this is a rate to watch for spikes, never an error count. A duplicate spike with flat persisted means redelivery.

panels.title: Dead letters by reason
panels.description: `unpersistable` is the one to read first: it includes a missing monthly partition, which dead-letters perfectly good events at full throughput. Dead letters expire with the topic's 7-day retention.

panels.title: DLQ replay
panels.description: `POST /admin/dlq/replay` on cobalt. Read this beside *Dead letters by reason*: a replay whose records come straight back to the DLQ is a poison loop and the fix was not the fix. `skipped` is the attempt ceiling (REPLAY_MAX_ATTEMPTS) refusing a record that has already been replayed too often — expected, not an error. Operations are what an operator asked for; records are what moved.

panels.title: Batch size
panels.description: Records per batch against `CONSUMER_BATCH_SIZE` (500). Small batches while lag grows mean the consumer is starved, not saturated — that distinction is the whole reason this meter exists, and it is a shift in the p50, which a mean hides.

panels.title: Scheduled maintenance
panels.description: `maintenance.job.duration` counts by outcome. With N replicas the healthy steady state is one success and N-1 skipped per tick — that ratio is the advisory lock working. No run of any outcome means the job thread is dead, and nothing else will say so. The p99 duration is ADR §12.4's tripwire: when the rollup refresh approaches its own interval, the materialized view has outgrown full refresh and wants incremental merge tables instead.

panels.title: Search latency — ferrite
panels.description: `search.query.duration` percentiles by query shape — which filter families the query used, never the filter values. The read pool sets statement_timeout = 2s server-side: anything slower than that was waiting for a connection, not for a query.

panels.title: HTTP request rate by service and outcome
panels.description: The one HTTP timer, identical in name and tags across Play, Vert.x/Tapir and Cask. /metrics and /health are excluded at the source, so this is user traffic only.

panels.title: Pool utilisation
panels.description: HikariCP's own binding. `active` against `max` is how full the pool is; a flat `active == max` with a non-zero `pending` is saturation, and no amount of index work fixes it.

panels.title: Waiting for a connection
panels.description: `pending` is the count of threads blocked in `getConnection`; `acquire` is how long that wait cost. Any sustained pending count means the queue moved out of the dispatcher you sized and into the pool, where `connection-timeout` is the only thing shedding load. Raise the pool and its dispatcher together — they must stay equal.

targets.expr: sum by (service, pool) (rate(hikaricp_connections_acquire_seconds_sum[$__rate_interval])) / clamp_min(sum by (service, pool) (rate(hikaricp_connections_acquire_seconds_count[$__rate_interval])), 0.001)

panels.title: Auth decisions by reason
panels.description: `auth.decisions` from wolfram and cobalt. **`bad-signature` at volume is an attack**; `expired` at volume is a client that stopped refreshing; `scope-missing` is a deployment that granted the wrong role. All three arrive as a bare 401/403 in `http.server.requests`, which is why this exists. `disabled` non-zero means AUTH_ENABLED=false reached an environment nobody intended.

panels.title: Refusal ratio
panels.description: Refusals as a fraction of all credential decisions. Forty refusals out of forty requests and forty out of four hundred thousand are not the same event — which is the whole reason accepted decisions are counted.

panels.title: Consumer state and checkpoint divergence
panels.description: `consume.running` is 0/1 and is what separates a **deliberate pause** from an outage: lag rising with it at 1 is a consumer that cannot keep up, at 0 it is somebody's maintenance window. `consume.checkpoint.divergence` must be **zero** — the offset and the rows it accounts for are written in one transaction, so a persistent gap means one of the two commits is failing.

panels.title: Lifecycle commands and decode cost
panels.description: `consume.lifecycle.commands` is the audit trail for an API that can stop ingestion and move offsets — an unexpected rate here is the first sign something automated is driving the pipeline. `skipped` means the command was a no-op. The decode p99 separates CPU on the stream's thread from the batch write's blocking round trip: when throughput drops, exactly one of them moved.

panels.title: Producers — what is actually being sent
Payload size
panels.description: `ingest.payload.bytes` percentiles, accepted events only. A p99 pressed against `max-event-bytes` (1 MiB) means producers are being refused; a p99 at a hundredth of it means the ceiling protects nothing and the broker's own limit is the real constraint.

panels.title: Producer clock skew
panels.description: `ingest.time.skew` — how far producers' `time` is from the ingest clock, split by direction. **This is the leading indicator for the partition failure.** `occurred_at` decides which monthly partition a row lands in, so a fleet drifting toward the clamp (24 h future / 90 d past) is a fleet about to be rejected wholesale — and that arrives as `invalid-attributes` with no hint that a clock is the cause.

panels.title: Batch document size
panels.description: `ingest.batch.events`. Distinct from payload bytes because one large event and two hundred small ones are the same bytes and completely different work — the second is two hundred sequential produces.

panels.title: Search results and pagination
panels.description: `search.results.returned` against `search.query.duration`: a slow query returning three rows and a slow query returning a full page are different problems. The continuation ratio says how often the *first* page failed to answer the question — a product signal, since keyset pagination is cheap at any depth.

panels.title: Live tail and rollup freshness
panels.description: `tail.connections` is a direct read on how much of the eight-connection read pool the live tail is holding — the thing to look at when search gets slow for reasons the search meters cannot explain. `rollup.staleness` is the reader's-eye view of a maintenance job that has stopped: the overview keeps serving numbers, they are simply old, and nothing raises an error. `-1` means the rollup is empty.

panels.title: Heap used vs max
panels.description: Heap only. The images set MaxRAMPercentage=70, so max should be ~70 % of the container's memory limit; if it is 25 % instead, conf/application.ini did not reach the JVM.

panels.title: GC pause and overhead
panels.description: Pause max per service, and `jvm_gc_overhead` as the fraction of CPU spent collecting. Pool names containing G1 confirm the collector; plain `Eden Space` means ergonomics fell back to Serial and the -XX:+UseG1GC flag was lost.

panels.title: CPU usage
panels.description: Process CPU as a fraction of the machine, per service, with the system figure for context.

panels.title: Threads
panels.description: Live platform threads and, on JDK 25, the virtual-thread counts from VirtualThreadMetrics. A climbing platform count on ferrite means work escaped the fixed search dispatcher.

panels.title: Allocation rate
panels.description: Bytes promoted out of the young generation per second. A step change here without a matching change in throughput is usually a new per-event allocation on the hot path.

panels.title: Uptime
panels.description: Restarts are visible as sawteeth. A service that restarts on a period is usually being killed by the container memory limit, not by its own ExitOnOutOfMemoryError.
